title: Water

notes.heading: 1. Temporary vs Permanent Hardness & CaCO₃ Equivalents (ppm)
notes.proseLatex: Hard water fails to lather with soap because $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ precipitate insoluble calcium/magnesium stearates ($2\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{35}\text{COONa} + \text{Ca}^{2+} \to (\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{35}\text{COO})_2\text{Ca}\downarrow$). TEMPORARY (carbonate) hardness comes from dissolved $\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2$ and $\text{Mg(HCO}_3)_2$, whereas PERMANENT (non-carbonate) hardness comes from $\text{CaCl}_2, \text{MgCl}_2, \text{CaSO}_4, \text{MgSO}_4$. Hardness is universally expressed in ppm ($\text{mg/L}$) of $\text{CaCO}_3$ equivalent because molar mass of $\text{CaCO}_3$ is a convenient $100\text{ g/mol}$ (equivalent weight $= 50$).

keyFormulas.label: CaCO₃ Equivalent Conversion & Hardness Units
keyFormulas.latex: $\text{Eq. of CaCO}_3 = W_{\text{salt}} \times \frac{100}{M_{\text{divalent salt}}},\qquad 1\text{ ppm} = 1\text{ mg/L} = 0.1^\circ\text{Fr} = 0.07^\circ\text{Cl}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Convert mg/L of CaSO4(136), MgSO4(120), CaCl2(111), MgCl2(95), Ca(HCO3)2(162) into ppm CaCO3.

examples.problemLatex: A water sample contains $13.6\text{ mg/L}$ of $\text{CaSO}_4$ ($M=136$) and $9.5\text{ mg/L}$ of $\text{MgCl}_2$ ($M=95$). Find its total hardness in ppm $\text{CaCO}_3$.
stepsLatex: $\text{MgCl}_2$ contribution $= 9.5 \times \frac{100}{95} = 10\text{ mg/L} = 10\text{ ppm}$, giving total hardness $= 20\text{ ppm}$.

notes.heading: 2. Boiling, Clark's Lime, Permutit (Zeolite), Calgon & Ion-Exchange Resins
notes.proseLatex: BOILING or Clark's calculated-lime method ($\text{Ca(OH)}_2$) removes ONLY temporary hardness ($\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CaCO}_3\downarrow + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$, while $\text{Mg(HCO}_3)_2$ precipitates as $\text{Mg(OH)}_2\downarrow$!). Permanent + temporary hardness are removed by: (a) Permutit/Zeolite ($\text{Na}_2\text{Ze}$, hydrated sodium aluminosilicate, regenerated by $10\%\text{ NaCl}$ brine), (b) Calgon ($\text{Na}_6\text{P}_6\text{O}_{18}$, sequesters $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ into soluble $[\text{Na}_2\text{CaP}_6\text{O}_{18}]^{2-}$), and (c) Ion-exchange resins ($\text{R-H}^+$ + $\text{R'-OH}^-$, yielding demineralized/deionized water removing ALL cations and anions!).

keyFormulas.label: Zeolite Softening, Regeneration & Calgon Complexation
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compare boiling, zeolite (leaves Na+ salts), Calgon, and mixed-bed deionization.

notes.heading: 3. EDTA Complexometric Titration, Potable Disinfection & BOD/COD
notes.proseLatex: Hardness is assayed quantitatively by complexometric titration with disodium EDTA at $\text{pH} \approx 10$ ($\text{NH}_4\text{OH}/\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ buffer) using Eriochrome Black-T (EBT) indicator: wine-red $[\text{Mg-EBT}]$ turns pure blue at the endpoint as EDTA forms stabler $1:1$ chelates with $\text{Ca}^{2+}/\text{Mg}^{2+}$. Municipal disinfection uses chlorination ($\text{HOCl}$ active germicide), bleaching powder ($\text{CaOCl}_2$), or ozonation; organic pollution is tracked via Biochemical Oxygen Demand ($\text{BOD}_5$ at $20^\circ\text{C}$) and Chemical Oxygen Demand ($\text{COD}$, acidic $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, always $\text{COD} \ge \text{BOD}$!).

keyFormulas.label: EDTA Titration Conditions & COD ≥ BOD
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Recall EBT colour change, pH 10 buffer, and why COD exceeds BOD.

wbjeebTraps: Boiling $\text{Mg(HCO}_3)_2$ precipitates $\text{Mg(OH)}_2\downarrow$ (because $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ has lower $K_{sp}$ than $\text{MgCO}_3$), whereas $\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2$ precipitates $\text{CaCO}_3\downarrow$!
Zeolite process removes hardness ($\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}$) but does NOT demineralize water ($\text{Na}^+$ salts remain in solution); ion-exchange resins remove ALL ions.
$\text{COD}$ is ALWAYS $\ge \text{BOD}$ because dichromate oxidizes both biodegradable and non-biodegradable organics.
